result:
I put the answer in `final.py`. It scores **84.5 on the search split**, meaning it runs about 84× faster than the reference, and I used **7 of the 24 scorer calls**.

It returns exactly the reference's pairs on everything I checked: 1,500 random small cases in my test harness, another 6,000 random small inputs with hand-picked edge cases, and 8 large inputs of 2,500–3,000 records. On 4 large inputs I never tuned on, it ran 65–66× faster than the reference, all with exact output.

I followed the skill's default budget of about 15 minutes, because you set none. The search ran from 14:31 to about 14:43, so it ended roughly 2–3 minutes early with 17 calls unused. The last three ideas each gained nothing locally, so I stopped there.

| | search score |
|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 |
| first champion (c1) | 63.5 |
| final pick (c9) | **84.5** |

**Why it's faster.** The reference compares every pair of records, about 4.5 million comparisons per input. The final version only compares pairs that could possibly reach 80%:
- **Exact duplicates first:** records with the same set of words are grouped once, and their pairs come straight from the groups.
- **Rare words first:** each record's words are sorted from rarest to most common across the whole input. Two records that are 80% alike must share at least two words among their first few. A lookup table built only from those first words finds the few hundred to thousand candidate pairs per input.
- **Size limits:** a record can only match records of 80–125% of its own word count. Records with 3 or fewer words can only match an identical record.
- **Exact check:** each remaining candidate gets the exact test from the specification, `5·|A∩B| ≥ 4·|A∪B|`.

**Other approaches tried:**
- Counting every shared word for every pair: correct but about 8× slower than the champion, dropped.
- Requiring 3 shared words instead of 2: 12% slower, dropped.
- Skipping words that appear only once: no change, dropped.
- Merging two loops (c9) gained about 1.5%, and storing words as numbers (c7) about 5%.
- c10 avoided importing `collections` and `bisect`. It measured 10% faster when each run starts a fresh Python process, but it didn't improve the scorer result (83.1). The scorer seems to have those modules loaded already, so I went back to the c9 version.

**Candidate log**

| candidate | change | harness | scorer | kept? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| c1 | rare-words-first lookup + exact-duplicate grouping | 63 ms | 63.5 | parent |
| c2 | faster candidate collection, size limits | 47 ms | – | parent |
| c3 | shorter lookup entries for smaller records | 41 ms | 70.7 | parent |
| c4 | faster word counting | ~same | – | merged |
| c5 | require 2 shared words | 43 ms (larger test set) | 71.7 | parent |
| c6 | 2-shared-word check done with set operations | 37 ms | 79.4 | parent |
| c7 | split once, records stored as sorted number tuples | 35 ms | 83.6 | parent |
| cd | count every shared word | 356 ms | – | dropped |
| c8 | skip words that appear only once | ±0 | – | dropped |
| **c9** | merge the lookup and insert loops | 34 ms | **84.5** | **final** |
| c10 | c9 without `collections`/`bisect` | slower in-process, faster fresh | 83.1 | dropped |
| c11 | require 3 shared words | +12% | – | dropped |
| c12 | cache method lookups | ±0 | – | dropped |

**The remaining cost** is basic Python work over each record: about 4 of the ~8 ms per input goes to splitting the text, building the word sets and sorting them. Further gains here will be small. I can't run your hidden final instances, so the final score may differ somewhat from 84.5. I've left my test files (`harness.py`, `bench.py`, `fresh.py`) and the candidates `c*.py` in the folder.
